pairing.target: Unlike earlier conquerors, Sargon simply annexed the Sumerian-Akkadian city-states, thereby creating the first centralized state in the history of Mesopotamia. Temple and state estates were entirely at the king’s disposal; the city-states were deprived of any traditional autonomy, and their rulers, henceforth styled only ensi, with Sargon now the sole lugal, effectively became royal officials. Councils of elders and popular assemblies ceased to function as governing bodies, although Sargon did convene assemblies of warriors, his supporters, and consulted them. Sargon’s successors even purchased land from the communities in a “voluntarily compulsory” manner at reduced prices, thereby expanding the state estate. The official language of Sargon’s dynasty was not only Sumerian but also Akkadian. The population as a whole, apart from those who had managed to enter the military-service stratum, gained little from Sargon’s victory because of state exploitation through corvée obligations and taxation.

pairing.target: In Old Babylonian Mesopotamia, three estates were distinguished: the free commoners, the avilum (“men”); the “king’s men,” the muškenum (“those who bow under someone’s protection”); and slaves by estate, the wardum. The avilum enjoyed communal self-government, although they paid tribute to the king. The muškenum did not belong to the communities. They placed themselves under the king’s protection in order to receive a plot of land from him, and lived separately, as small holdings on royal land; on them lay the main burden of taxation. In addition, special groups of muškenum performed military service as military colonists or held other royal service. Their lives were regulated by the state. Unlike the avilum, the muškenum were, for the most part, unable to leave the land on which they lived without state permission. People settled on state land on condition that they surrender a share of the harvest (the sources know them by the name nāši biltim, “revenue payers”; overwhelmingly, these were muškenum) were the chief source of state income. The wardum were private slaves, bought and sold. The estates were unequal before the law: murder of an avilum was punishable by death, whereas one who killed a slave needed only to compensate the owner for the loss, and so on. Yet there were no rigid boundaries, including psychological ones, between the estates: in Mesopotamia it was always assumed that, despite differences in status, people were by nature little different from one another. A slave could possess property of his own and have a family; the master ordinarily controlled only his time and labor. For this reason, the Laws of Hammurabi even had to include a special article threatening a free person with severe punishment for helping a fugitive slave.

According to geological research, in the postglacial period the Great Plain was largely inundated by rising waters of the World Ocean and began to emerge only from the mid-6th millennium BCE, owing to the heavy alluviation of the Yellow River and the rivers of the Shandong archipelago. As a distinct zone, the Great Plain took shape only by the beginning of the 2nd millennium BCE, and its development lasted for centuries, determining the possibilities for the rapid rise of Hua-Xia statehood in the second half of the 1st millennium BCE and for the creation of an empire dominated by the Han ethnos at the end of antiquity (3rd century BCE–3rd century CE). This concept of the formation of the Great Plain offers a new understanding of the historical process in the eastern part of the Old World.
